newsitem.title: MALI: President's party ahead in Mali parliament poll.
newsitem.headline: President's party ahead in Mali parliament poll.

text.p: Supporters of President Alpha Oumar Konare took an early lead on Monday as results from Mali's chaotic weekend parliamentary election trickled out.

Independent National Electoral Commission (CENI) officials told reporters that Konare supporters were ahead in six towns for which results from Sunday's election were available but that most seats there would be decided in an April 27 runoff.
Elsewhere, the West African nation counted the democratic cost of Sunday's chaotic poll.

Voters flocked to polling stations for Sunday's election, which launched the impoverished nation's second multi-party national elections since independence from France in 1960, only to find that organisational glitches prevented them from voting.

"Given the crowds at polling stations...one cannot help but regret that that indescribable chaos there cooled the civic enthusiasm of the people of Bamako which could have resulted in a high turnout," the government daily L'Essor commented.

Sunday's poll for a new 147-seat national assembly, and presidential and municipal elections in May and June are a test of how deeply democracy has taken root in Mali, which won widespread praise for its 1992 democratic transition.
Konare's ADEMA alliance notched up tallies ranging from 29 to 61 percent, but in all but one town -- Kangaba -- its party lists failed to achieve the outright majority needed to win seats.
Opposition politician Mohamedoun Dicko, a one-time Konare supporter, told an independent radio station that the opposition was considering legal challenges to the poll.

Dicko, whose MIRIA party belongs to one of two opposition alliances, blamed the government. "They do not care about consolidating the democratic process which was installed in Mali at the cost of bloodshed," he said.
Independent newspapers deplored lack of polling materials and problems with voter cards and lists.
Most of the 1,500 candidates from 21 parties who contested the election were supporters of Konare, a historian elected in 1992, or candidates from two main opposition alliances.
Landlocked on the edge of the Sahara desert, Mali has few natural advantages apart from gold -- a sector it is expanding.
